918.title: Namdev
918.howItsDone: Varkari devotees in Maharashtra sing Namdev's songs to Vitthal, and Sikhs read and sing the hymns under his name in the Guru Granth Sahib, where his words are kept beside those of the Gurus.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Namdev, called half-baked by a potter, learned from Visoba Khechar's feet that there's nowhere without God.

Lunch is laid out: a few pieces of flatbread, and a little pot of ghee, clarified butter, to spread on top. Namdev looks away for a moment. A stray dog trots in, snatches the bread, and runs. Namdev jumps up and goes after it. Not with a stick. He's carrying the pot of ghee, calling: wait, that bread is dry, let me butter it for you. That's the story told about him.
screen: `A DOG STEALS THE BREAD.` → `NAMDEV CHASES IT.` → `HE'S CARRYING THE GHEE.`

segments.voice: Visoba taught Namdev that there's no place without God. Here is that lesson trotting off on four legs. Someone who has really learned it can't see a hungry dog as only a thief. In the story, Namdev sees Vitthal in it, and the one problem left is that the bread is dry. Some tellings say Vitthal then shows himself, smiling. Now a harder story. Namdev goes to a temple to sing; tradition places it at Aundha. The priests push him out. In their eyes, a man of his birth doesn't belong there. So Namdev walks around to the back, sits on the ground, and keeps singing. And the story says the temple turned, the whole building swinging around until its door faced Namdev and its back faced the priests. This one Namdev tells himself, in a hymn kept under his name in the Guru Granth Sahib, the scripture of the Sikhs. Roughly, he says he came to the temple laughing and playing, was seized and driven out because of the community he was born into, and the temple turned to face him. So his own words sit inside the Sikh scripture, beside the hymns of the Gurus. Put the two stories side by side. In the first, God is so near that even a dog with stolen lunch is him. In the second, God won't stay in a building that sends his singer away. Both times, God comes around to wherever Namdev already is.
screen: `THE LESSON ON FOUR LEGS.` · `PUSHED OUT OF THE TEMPLE.` · `THE TEMPLE TURNS.` · then, large: `A HYMN IN THE GURU GRANTH SAHIB.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one creature that annoyed you lately: a neighbor's dog, a pigeon on the sill, someone who took the last cup of coffee. Hold them without the annoyance and ask Namdev's question: if this one were holy too, what would I hand them? Let the answer stay small, just the ghee for the bread, and if you pray, hold them before God.
Namdev. The poet-saint of Pandharpur who chased a dog to butter its bread, and whose hymn of the turning temple is kept in the Guru Granth Sahib.
Your line: the butter, not the stick. Even a thief with your lunch can be met with ghee. Day nine hundred eighteen, done.

919.title: Tukaram
919.carry: one for you and one for me
919.howItsDone: Tukaram belongs to the Varkari tradition of Maharashtra; Varkaris sing his songs to Vitthal at home and in temples, and the stories of his life are told and retold among them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Namdev chased a dog with the butter, and sang behind a temple until, the story says, it turned to face him.

A man walks home along a village road with an armful of sugarcane, a gift from a farmer whose field he'd been helping with. You peel it and chew it for the sweet juice. Children see him coming and run up. Can we have some? He hands one stalk to the first child. Then the next, and the next. By the time he reaches his own door, he's holding a single stalk. Waiting inside is his wife, with a household to feed. The man is Tukaram.
screen: `AN ARMFUL OF SUGARCANE.` → `THE CHILDREN ASK.` → `ONE STALK LEFT.`

segments.voice: Tukaram is remembered as a grocer in the village of Dehu, on the Indrayani river, a devotee of Vitthal, the same god Namdev sang to. Tradition ties the two together: it says Namdev came to Tukaram in a dream, with Vitthal beside him, and set him the task of making songs. And the songs came. The stories don't pretend his life was easy. Tradition says his shop failed, famine hit his region, and he lost people he loved. Out of that grief, the stories say, he turned his whole life toward Vitthal. Back to the door, and the one stalk. His wife is furious. Tradition remembers her as sharp-tongued, but the story is fair to her: the family is poor, and her husband keeps giving everything away. She grabs the last stalk and brings it down across his back. It snaps in two. And Tukaram, rubbing his shoulder, looks at the pieces and says something like: wonderful, now there's one for you and one for me. It's funny. It's also a man who has decided, all the way down, that nothing he's handed is his to hoard, not the cane, not even the moment of being hit. The anger doesn't get a fight back. It gets half the sugarcane. His Varkari tradition doesn't ask anyone to leave home for a cave. It holds up people like this: a grocer, a husband, with debts and a hungry household at the door, singing to Vitthal right in the middle of it.
screen: `A GROCER OF DEHU.` · `NAMDEV IN A DREAM.` · `THE STALK SNAPS IN TWO.` · then, large: `ONE FOR YOU AND ONE FOR ME.`

segments.voice: Let your shoulders drop, and think of something you were handed lately, time, money, patience, that you gave away along the road before it reached the people at home. Don't scold yourself or defend yourself; just notice where it went, and who is waiting at your own door. If you pray, you can hold both the road and the door before God.
Tukaram. The grocer-saint of Dehu who gave away the sugarcane on the road home, and split the last broken stalk with the wife who broke it.
Your line: one for you and one for me. Even a broken stalk can be shared. Until tomorrow.

920.title: Tukaram
920.tomorrow: Kabir (the dohas, one a day for a week)
920.howItsDone: Varkaris sing Tukaram's abhangs in kirtan and on the yearly walking pilgrimage to Pandharpur, when a palanquin carrying his sandals travels from Dehu with the pilgrims.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Tukaram split the last broken stalk of sugarcane with his wife. One for you, one for me.
screen: `TUKARAM.` · `ONE FOR YOU AND ONE FOR ME.`

segments.voice: On the bank of the Indrayani, a man holds a bundle of handwritten notebooks full of songs. He steps to the edge and lets them go. They sink into the brown water and are gone. Nobody stole them or tore them up. He was told to do this, and he did it himself. Then he sits down on the bare ground by the water, and he doesn't get up.
screen: `A BUNDLE OF NOTEBOOKS.` → `INTO THE RIVER.` → `HE SITS DOWN ON THE BANK.`

segments.voice: The songs are abhangs, the short devotional verses of the Varkari saints, made to be sung in Marathi, the everyday language Jnaneshwar had already opened the Gita in. Tukaram made them for Vitthal, and people sang them. Not everyone was pleased. Tradition names a learned man, Rameshwar Bhatt, who objected that a grocer had no business composing songs about sacred things, and in everyday Marathi at that. The story says he ordered Tukaram to sink his notebooks in the river. And Tukaram did. He doesn't argue, hide a copy, or run to another town. He obeys, then sits on the bank and refuses food, turning it all over to Vitthal. If the songs were his, let them drown. If they were Vitthal's, let Vitthal decide. Days go by. Then, tradition says, the notebooks rose to the surface of the Indrayani, dry, and were carried back to him. The story goes one step further: the man who gave the order fell ill, and was healed only after he came to Tukaram and became his follower. It isn't told as a victory over an enemy, but as two people both changed by the songs. Whatever happened at that river, the songs did not drown. Varkaris still sing Tukaram's abhangs. In the season of the great walking pilgrimage to Pandharpur, a palanquin carrying his sandals sets out from Dehu, and the pilgrims walking with it sing his words along the road.
screen: `ABHANGS, IN THE LANGUAGE OF HOME.` · `SINK THEM IN THE RIVER.` · `HE SITS AND WAITS.` · then, large: `THE NOTEBOOKS RISE.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands open in your lap and think of one thing you made that you're anxious about: a project, a letter, even a reputation. Imagine setting it on the water, not destroying it, only letting go of having to protect it, and notice what it feels like to sit on the bank with empty hands. If you pray, you can leave it with God for these few minutes.
Tukaram. The grocer-saint of Dehu who sank his songs in the Indrayani when he was told to, and sat on the bank until, tradition says, they rose.
Your line: the notebooks rise. A man let go of everything he'd written, and the singing went on anyway. That's day nine hundred twenty.

921.title: Kabir (the dohas, one a day for a week)
921.hook: Kabir (the dohas, one a day for a week)
921.tomorrow: Kabir (the dohas, one a day for a week)
921.howItsDone: Kabir's dohas are sung and quoted by followers of the Kabir Panth, in Hindu devotional singing, and in everyday talk; his verses are also kept in the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Tukaram sank his notebooks in the Indrayani and sat on the bank until, tradition says, they rose dry.

Before dawn, on the stone steps that run down to the Ganges at Kashi, a young weaver lies stretched across a step in the dark. He knows a famous teacher, Ramananda, comes down here to bathe at this hour. The teacher's foot comes down on him. Startled, Ramananda cries out the name of God: Ram, Ram. And the young man goes home holding those words as if they'd been handed to him on purpose. That, tradition says, is how Kabir got his teacher.
screen: `STEPS DOWN TO THE GANGES.` → `A FOOT IN THE DARK.` → `RAM, RAM.`

segments.voice: Kabir is remembered as a weaver in Kashi, raised, tradition says, by a Muslim weaver couple, Niru and Nima, who found him as a baby by a pond. A man between worlds, who spent his life making cloth and making songs. He left a particular kind of song: the doha. A couplet, two lines that rhyme, short enough to remember after one hearing, sharp enough to keep working on you. Kabir's dohas are passed along by people singing and quoting them, and they're best taken one at a time. Today's begins, in Hindi, bura jo dekhan main chala. Roughly: I went out looking for the bad one, and couldn't find anyone. Then I searched my own heart, and found no one worse than me. Notice the trick. The first line starts on a familiar hunt: who's the problem in this office, this family, this group chat? Found nobody. The second line turns the lamp around. It doesn't say you're terrible. It says the search only works in one direction, inward, and that's where the material is. Kabir doesn't argue. He sets a little trap in two lines, and the listener walks into it and springs it. Later, when the hunt for someone to blame starts up again, the second line can come back by itself. That's what a doha is for.
screen: `A WEAVER OF KASHI.` · `THE DOHA: TWO LINES THAT RHYME.` · `I WENT LOOKING FOR THE BAD ONE.` · then, large: `I SEARCHED MY OWN HEART.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you've been quietly blaming lately, and let the case against them come up as it usually does. Then gently turn the lamp around and ask: what did I bring to this? Not to take all the blame, just to see your own part as clearly as you saw theirs; if you pray, you can hold what you found before God.
Kabir. The weaver-poet of Kashi whose dohas, two rhyming lines, set little traps. Today's: I went looking for the bad one, and searched my own heart.
Your line: I searched my own heart. The search only works turned inward. See you tomorrow.

922.title: Kabir (the dohas, one a day for a week)
922.hook: Kabir (the dohas, one a day for a week)
922.tomorrow: Kabir (the dohas, one a day for a week)
922.howItsDone: This doha of Kabir is quoted in Hindi homes and classrooms as a saying about love and learning, and is sung in devotional settings by those who keep Kabir's songs.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kabir's first doha. I went looking for the bad one, found no one, then searched my own heart.

A shelf sags under the weight of books, commentaries on commentaries. A scholar has spent his life there, and he can quote line and verse on anything you ask. Down the lane, a weaver throws the shuttle back and forth at his loom. Tradition says he never learned to read. He has a two-line answer for the man with the shelf, about how much reading it takes to become wise. His count is very small.
screen: `A SHELF OF BOOKS.` → `A WEAVER AT HIS LOOM.` → `A VERY SMALL COUNT.`

segments.voice: Today's doha begins, in Hindi, pothi padh padh jag mua. A pothi is a book, a sacred text, and the line says, roughly: reading book after book, the whole world died, and not one became a pandit, a truly learned one. Then the second line: whoever reads the two and a half letters of love becomes the pandit. Two and a half letters is the doha's own count, and one common reading makes it a joke you can see on the page. The Hindi word for love, prem, is written with a half letter joined to the front of a full one, and then one more. So all the learning the scholar spent his life on fits in a word you can write in a second and spend a lifetime learning to read. Kabir doesn't say books are bad; his own verses ended up in books. He says something narrower and sharper: reading alone doesn't finish anyone. You can read about love until you die, and never once read love itself, the way it's written in a face, in a neighbor's need, in God. And here's the trap, like yesterday's. Some readers stop at the first line, pleased: ha, all those books. But the second line asks something of them too. Have you read the two and a half letters? Not heard of them. Read them. In Kabir's picture, love is the text, every day is the exam, and the exam isn't on paper.
screen: `READING BOOK AFTER BOOK.` · `NOT ONE BECAME A PANDIT.` · `TWO AND A HALF LETTERS.` · then, large: `WHOEVER READS LOVE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person whose love you had to learn to read, someone who shows it sideways: a grandparent who fed you instead of talking, a friend who teases, a parent who worries out loud. Picture how they actually show it, and read it slowly, letter by letter, like something precious. If you pray, you can thank God for them in whatever words you already use.
Kabir. The weaver-poet of Kashi. Today's doha: reading book after book, no one became wise; whoever reads the two and a half letters of love becomes the pandit.
Your line: two and a half letters. All that learning fits in one small word. Day nine hundred twenty-two, done.

923.title: Kabir (the dohas, one a day for a week)
923.hook: Kabir (the dohas, one a day for a week)

923.tomorrow: Tulsidas (the Ramcharitmanas opening and the Hanuman Chalisa, verse by verse)
923.howItsDone: The musk deer doha is quoted as a saying about looking for God far away, and the story of the flowers under Kabir's sheet is told by people of more than one community who honor him.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kabir's second doha. No one became wise from books alone; whoever reads the two and a half letters of love becomes the pandit.

A deer moves through the forest, head low, nose working. There's a scent in the air, rich and sweet, and it's maddening, because it's everywhere and nowhere. The deer checks behind a tree. Under a bush. Down by the stream. The scent is just as strong in each place, and never any closer. It keeps searching until it's worn out. Kabir put this deer in two lines. It's the third doha this week, and the last day with the weaver of Kashi.
screen: `A SCENT IN THE FOREST.` → `EVERYWHERE AND NOWHERE.` → `THE DEER KEEPS SEARCHING.`

segments.voice: The doha begins, in Hindi, kasturi kundal basai. Kasturi is musk, the prized scent. Roughly: the musk lives in the deer's own navel, and the deer goes searching for it through the forest. Then the second line: just so, Ram is in every body, every heart, and the world doesn't see. The joke is gentle, and the deer stands for anyone who searches. Every place smelled of musk because the deer brought it to every place. Ram, in Kabir's mouth, is the name his teacher cried out on the steps at Kashi. But Kabir's Ram isn't held in one temple or one image. In this doha, Ram is in every heart, and the trouble is only that people look everywhere else first. Put the three dohas together. Go looking for the bad one, and you end up searching your own heart. Read book after book, and the lesson is still two and a half letters, love. Search the whole forest for God, and the scent was in you all along. Three hunts, each turning back toward the hunter. Kabir's life ends, tradition says, with one more turn. When he died, his followers, Hindus and Muslims, each wanted to give him their own last rites. Some say they argued over the body. When they lifted the sheet, there was no body at all, only a heap of flowers. So each group took half the flowers, and honored him in its own way.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kabir's last doha. The musk is in the deer, and Ram is in every heart.

It's night, and the river is high from the rains. A young man comes home to find his wife gone to her parents' house across the water, and he can't stand to wait until morning. So he crosses the swollen river in the dark and climbs up to her window. She is not charmed. She's embarrassed, and tells him so, sharply: if you loved Ram the way you love this body of flesh and bone, you'd be free. The young man goes away and doesn't come back. That's how tradition tells the turning of Tulsidas.
screen: `A SWOLLEN RIVER AT NIGHT.` → `HIS WIFE'S SHARP WORDS.` → `HE TURNS TO RAM.`

segments.voice: Tulsidas became a poet of Ram, and his great work is the Ramcharitmanas, the story of Ram retold in Awadhi, a language people spoke, not the Sanskrit of the older Ramayana. The poem opens with a short run of Sanskrit verses, as if Tulsidas bows at the threshold in the old language before stepping inside in the new one. The very first verse bows to Vani, the goddess of speech, and to Vinayaka, Ganesha: makers of letters and meanings, of the flavors and meters of verse, and of everything auspicious. Before writing a word, the poet thanks the one who gives words, and the one who clears the road. Then comes a line that's easy to miss. Tulsidas says why he writes: for the happiness of his own heart, svantah sukhaya. Not for fame. He tells Ram's story because telling it makes him glad. And the poem explains its own name. It says Shiva composed this story first and kept it in his own mind, his manas, so it's called the Manas of Ram's deeds. Tulsidas says he's passing on something Shiva has held in his heart. Look back at this week. Namdev, a dog and a turning temple. Tukaram's split sugarcane and his notebooks rising from the river. Kabir's three dohas, each turning the hunt back on the hunter. And Tulsidas, turned around by his wife's sharp words, sitting down to write for the joy of it.
screen: `THE MANAS, IN AWADHI.` · `A BOW TO VANI AND VINAYAKA.` · `FOR MY OWN HEART'S JOY.` · then, large: `KEPT IN SHIVA'S MIND.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you do, or used to do, simply because it makes you glad: singing in the car, cooking, telling a story to a child. Let it come back with its sound and its feel, and notice what happens inside you. Then, the way Tulsidas bowed before he started, be thankful for whatever gave you that gift, and if you pray, offer that thanks to God.
Tulsidas. The poet of the Ramcharitmanas, who bowed to Vani and Vinayaka at its door, and wrote the story of Ram for the happiness of his own heart.
Your line: for my own heart's joy. Svantah sukhaya: he wrote for gladness, not for fame. Until tomorrow.
